back: The net movement of particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration. It doesn't need energy from the cell.
The diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one.
Moving particles from low to high concentration (against the concentration gradient), using energy from respiration.
A difference in concentration between two areas. The steeper the gradient, the faster the diffusion.
A membrane that lets small molecules, like water, through but not larger ones, like sugar.

front: Four things that make diffusion faster
back: Higher temperature, bigger concentration difference, shorter distance and larger surface area.
Turgid: firm, with the vacuole full of water pushing on the cell wall. Flaccid: floppy, because the cell has lost water.

front: What happens to an animal cell in pure water?
back: Water enters by osmosis, so it swells and may burst. It has no cell wall to stop it.

front: Surface area and volume of a cube with side $L$
What happens to the SA:V ratio as an object gets bigger?
back: It gets smaller. Small objects have a large SA:V ratio.
A small cell has a large SA:V ratio and short distances, so substances can diffuse in and out fast enough to supply the whole cell.

front: Examples of exchange surfaces with a large surface area
back: Alveoli (lungs), villi (small intestine), root hairs (roots) and gills (fish).
Root hair cells taking in mineral ions from the soil; the small intestine absorbing glucose.

front: Diffusion vs active transport: direction and energy
back: Diffusion: high → low concentration, no energy needed. Active transport: low → high concentration, needs energy.
